groups.text: A fraud check loads the reference in a merchant object, and follows it to a risk score.
To empty this region, the collector copies the risk score out.
But the merchant still holds the old address.
So the usual collector stops every thread, copies, fixes every reference, and only then lets them run.
In lesson four's G one log, that pause took sixteen ms, almost all of it copying.
On a thirty-two GB heap, a full G C can stop for seconds: an outage for a fraud check with a twenty ms budget.
How could the collector move objects while the threads keep running?
Z G C adds two things.
Every reference in the heap carries a few extra bits: its color.
After every reference load, the jit adds a check: the load barrier.
It compares that color with the one the collector calls good right now.
Nearly always they match: a test and a branch.
Now the collector changes the good color, and copies the risk score while the thread runs on.
The next load sees an old color, so the barrier takes the slow path.
It finds the new address, and writes the fixed reference back into the merchant.
The load after that is fast again.
So Z G C stops threads only to handle their roots: three pauses per collection, about zero point zero two ms each in the demo, while the zero point zero five two s collection runs beside them.
The price: eight-byte references, so a forty-byte Payment takes forty-eight.
C P U for G C threads and barriers.
And headroom, or allocating threads stall.
Most services stay on G one.
Pick Z G C when pauses must stay under about ten ms, and cores are spare.
Shenandoah makes the same trade.
Serial fits one C P U, Parallel fits batch jobs, and Epsilon is only for tests.
The rule: Z G C moves objects while your threads run, because a barrier on every reference load fixes stale references.
You pay in C P U and memory.
Quick check. The barrier just fixed the merchant's field.
What does the next load cost?
A test and a branch.
Its color is good again.
